issues.issue: Acreage-basis allocation of royalty on pooled production is hard to square with Paragraph 3(g)'s statement that shut-in payments "shall not be subject to proportionate reduction" for a well on a pooled unit. Whether the acreage fraction applies to shut-in royalty as well as production royalty is unresolved.

Saying unpooled land may be maintained "in any manner provided in this Lease" runs against Paragraphs 4(d) and 4(h), which terminate the lease as to all land outside a producing or drilling unit after continuous drilling ends. The two leave it doubtful whether unpooled acreage survives.

The mandatory duty to commence an offset well within 120 days is immediately qualified by "as a reasonable and prudent operator would drill under the same or similar circumstances," so it is unclear whether the obligation is absolute or excused by prudent-operator judgment. The trigger distance "within three hundred thirty feet (330') of the Leased Premises" also does not say whether the measure runs from the well or the unit.

The presumption applies to wells producing "within these defined distances," plural, although the preceding sentence states only one distance (330 feet). The plural reference leaves the presumption's reach uncertain.

"Lessee shall either" (a) pay compensatory royalties or (b) release does not say who elects, or whether the two listed remedies are exclusive of damages for breach of the offset covenant. The expressio unius reading of the enumerated remedies is squarely arguable.

The further-development covenant is measured only by what "a reasonable and prudent operator would" do, with no well count, timetable or acreage benchmark. Whether it adds anything to the implied covenant, and when it is breached, cannot be told from the words.

Requiring Lessee to conduct "all operations hereunder at its sole cost, risk and expense" is in tension with Paragraph 3(b), which lets Lessee net certain regulated transportation charges against royalty proceeds. Whether post-production activities are "operations hereunder" borne solely by Lessee is the question a royalty-deduction dispute would raise.

The indemnity covers claims "arising from any causes whatsoever" without excepting Lessor's own negligence, so whether it indemnifies Lessor against its own fault is open. Arkansas requires clear expression for such coverage, and this clause never names negligence.

Lessor reserves "geothermal energy (including entrained methane, hydrostatic pressure and thermal energy)" and "any other mineral substances," while Paragraph 1 grants Lessee "gas and respective constituent products" from the same land. Ownership of methane entrained in water or coal, and of casinghead constituents, is left contradictory between the grant and the reservation.

"[N]ot to unreasonably interfere with the operations or activities of the other" supplies no priority rule where Lessor's reserved-mineral lessees and Lessee's drilling genuinely conflict. "Unreasonably" is the undefined term carrying the whole obligation.

The clause says assignment "may" be made freely, then conditions it on Lessor's consent, but states as the only consequence of assigning without consent that Lessee "remain[s] liable" — leaving unclear whether consent is truly required or merely a release mechanism. The trailing exception for "conveyance to officers of Lessee" is a further unexplained carve-out.

Insulating compliant segregated parts from another assignee's default is difficult to square with the same paragraph's rule that Lessee remains liable for the performance of its assignee's obligations after a non-consented assignment. Whose default forfeits which acreage is left contradictory.

"Notwithstanding the foregoing" does not identify what in Paragraph 11 it overrides — the free assignability, the consent requirement, or Lessee's continuing liability. Read with Paragraph 11, it is unclear whether an assignee's assumption of surface and subsurface damage liability displaces Lessee's own.

The indemnity covers claims "relating to such operations of Lessee," but the antecedent sentence speaks of compliance with laws, so "such operations" has no clear referent. Its overlap with the fuller indemnity in Paragraph 9 leaves the scope of protection uncertain.

Force majeure suspends only "the running of any period described in Paragraphs 4(a), (b) or (e)," enumerating three periods and thereby excluding the shut-in periods of 3(g), the offset deadline of Paragraph 6 and the periods in 4(d) and 4(f). Whether that list is exhaustive is precisely the expressio unius question.

The definition ends with the catch-all "any other cause not reasonably within Lessee's control" after a list of physical and regulatory events, raising an ejusdem generis question about economic causes such as low prices or lack of pipeline capacity. "Inability to obtain necessary permits, equipment, services" likewise has no boundary of commercial reasonableness.

The promise that nothing herein shall "penalize Lessee for complying" with laws or regulations cannot be squared with the fixed royalty and payment obligations of Paragraph 3, which regulatory compliance may make costly. How far regulatory compliance excuses lease obligations is left open.

The six-month cumulative cap is tied to suspensions "during the Primary Term," while the earlier part of Paragraph 13 suspends the post-primary-term periods of 4(a), (b) and (e). Whether the cap limits those post-term suspensions too, or only extension of the Primary Term, is ambiguous.

The daily-report duty here is stated in general terms, while Section 15 and Exhibit "B" prescribe the form and channel for the same information ("transmitted by email," composite reports, hard copies). Which specification governs the content and timing of daily reports is unresolved.

The duty to divulge "true and correct information as requested by Lessor" as to lithology and formations collides with the later sentence of Section 15 barring Lessor from "any interpretive data, materials, reports, maps or records." What technical information must actually be handed over falls between the two.

The absolute bar on access to "any interpretive data, materials, reports, maps or records" cannot be squared with Exhibit "B," incorporated by the last sentence of Section 15, which requires delivery of "interpretive logs (MRI, NMR etc)" and of "pressure transient data and interpretations thereof." One provision withholds what the other compels.

Confidentiality lasts "for so long as Lessee maintains such information as confidential," a condition Lessor cannot verify and that has no stated endpoint. The stockholder-reporting exception is likewise untethered to any standard of necessity.

Permitting Lessor to "use such information in its ordinary course of business" undercuts the confidentiality obligation imposed in the immediately preceding sentence of Section 15. Which of the two governs disclosure to Lessor's own lessees, purchasers or advisers is unsettled.

Making the Exhibit "B" Data Requirement Form govern "all information required pursuant to this Section 15" imports items that Section 15 elsewhere denies Lessor (interpretive logs) and items Section 15 never mentions (title opinions, drilling permits). Whether the Exhibit expands or merely formats the Section 15 duties is the conflict.

Proportionate reduction of "the royalties provided in this Lease" sits against Paragraph 3(g)'s statement that shut-in payments "shall not be subject to proportionate reduction." Whether shut-in royalty is a "royalt[y] provided in this Lease" for this purpose must be construed.

The confidentiality obligation runs "for so long as Lessee maintains such information as confidential," except where Lessor "in its sole opinion" must report to stockholders — a wholly subjective release from a duty of indefinite duration. Neither side of the standard is measurable.

Division and transfer orders are said to serve "solely for the purposes of confirming the extent of Lessor's interest," which does not say whether they may nevertheless govern the manner of payment or bind Lessor to a stated decimal. The interaction with the royalty valuation terms of Paragraph 3 is left unstated.

Requiring every alteration to be in a writing "executed by the party against whom" it is enforced cannot be squared with Paragraph 19, which lets Lessor unilaterally execute and file a release that "shall be binding upon Lessee." One provision forbids what the other authorizes.

Notice is effective "on the date personally delivered and/or received by the addressee," and the "and/or" leaves it unclear whether delivery alone or actual receipt fixes the date. The qualifier "unless otherwise specified" also does not identify where else the lease specifies otherwise.

Mailed notice by certified mail is prescribed here, but the first sentence of Paragraph 18 makes notice effective only on personal delivery and/or receipt by the addressee. Whether proper mailing or actual receipt completes notice is contradictory between the two sentences.

Making notice "in any other manner" effective only on receipt sits against Paragraph 13 (force majeure notice "in writing or by fax") and Paragraph 14 (fax or email drilling reports), which authorize other methods without saying when they take effect. The same sentence also appears twice in Paragraph 18, obscuring its intended scope.

Lessee must act "promptly" to prepare and file the release, but only the duty to forward a recorded copy carries the thirty-day deadline. When the release itself becomes overdue is therefore undefined.

"[F]ail to timely file an appropriate release instrument within thirty (30) days" does not say whether the thirty days runs from Lessor's written request or from the termination date fixed in the preceding sentence. The self-help release is triggered by an unfixed date.

Retention of roads, pipelines and installations lasts only "so long as such roads, pipelines and installations are useful in Lessee's operations under this Lease," with "useful" left undefined and unilaterally judged. It is also unclear what survives once the lease has terminated as to all remaining acreage.

Fees are payable if "the dispute is resolved in favor of Lessor," which says nothing about partial success, settlement, or a Lessor recovery smaller than claimed. The condition triggering the fee shift is the ambiguous term.

Insurance is required "[d]uring the Term of this Lease," while Exhibit "C" requires coverage "at all times while conducting operations under this Agreement." The two periods differ, notably for operations retained under Paragraph 20 after partial termination.

The lease is made "specifically subject to" an unrecorded March 30, 2006 letter agreement that is not attached and whose terms are unknown from this instrument, with no rule of priority if the two conflict. Read with Paragraph 17's requirement that amendments be in a writing describing the specific provisions affected, the letter's effect on the lease is squarely open.

Item 4's demand for "interpretive logs (MRI, NMR etc)" and item 5's demand for "interpretations thereof" cannot be reconciled with Section 15's provision that "in no event shall Lessor have any access to any interpretive data, materials, reports, maps or records." The Exhibit requires delivery of the very category the body withholds.

The limits column places "$1,000,000 Combined single limit" opposite subitem (b) contractual liability only, leaving subitem (a) property damage and bodily injury with no stated limit. Whether the $1,000,000 applies to the whole Comprehensive General Liability coverage or only to assumed contractual liability is unclear from the layout.
